title: Pilot scope: inference footprint & signal map - Horizon Logistics
summary: Initial POC scoping for an inference pilot: map traffic surface, define QPS/concurrency targets, token distribution profiling, benchmark KPIs (P50/P95/P99 latency, throughput), security and data residency constraints, and pilot timeline. Agreement on a 3-week pilot with a two-phase benchmark (synthetic replay + live shadowing). Action items assigned.

transcript:
Header:
Date: 2027-05-18
Start time: 15:00 PT
Duration: 62 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Ethan Cho (Redwood SE), Carlos Mendoza (CTO, Horizon), Aisha Khan (ML Lead), Liam O'Donnell (Infra)

Auto-summary (auto):
- High level: scope pilot to validate latency & cost tradeoffs for their real-time routing assistant; measure P99 tail under bursts and multi-tenant noise; characterize token distribution to pick quantization profile.
- Pilot plan: two-phase — synthetic replay benchmarks then 48h live shadowing behind their router. Acceptance: P99 <= 450ms for 90% of queries in peak bursts, throughput to sustain 1.2x targeted QPS during 5-minute bursts.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intros? we have ethan on the line from redis--- sorry, redwood infra.
[00:05] Ethan: hi all, hello.
[00:06] Carlos: carlos here, CTO at horizon logistics. we've been noodling on using LLMs for our dispatcher assistant, mostly latency sensitive.
[00:12] Aisha: aisha, ml lead — we manage the model training and infra ops.
[00:15] Liam: liam — infra, network, security.
[00:17] Maya: great. goal for today is to map your traffic shape and agree on success criteria and a benchmark cadence for the pilot. estimate 6-8 weeks from pilot kickoff to production ramp if all goes well, but we want to be concrete on the pilot scope first.

[02:05] Carlos: quick background — we have an edge fleet that sends routing queries to a central service. typical steady qps about 120 req/s globally, with morning and evening peaks of 450 req/s for 10-12 minutes; these are bursty. payloads are short: 20-60 tokens input, responses anywhere 30-400 tokens depending on the plan.

[03:15] Maya: ok that token spread is helpful — 30-400 output is a wide tail; we'll need to look at median and 95th percentiles. how sensitive are you to 95 vs 99?

[03:45] Aisha: we care about p99 because an occasional 2-3 second stall creates bad UX for drivers. target is p99 under peak bursts around 400-500ms, otherwise drivers get frustrated.

[04:20] Ethan: couple clarifying q's — is that 400-500ms end-to-end (app -> inference) or just model server?

[04:28] Carlos: that's apparent end-to-end from the app. network typically adds 50-80ms in our regions; so model-side p99 should be in the 300-420ms range.

[05:05] Liam: we run in GCP us-central, public subnets but with VPC peering available. if you do a private deployment we can consider dedicated peering, but at minimum egress cost and VPC firewall rules apply.

[06:00] Maya: good to note. for the pilot we recommend a hosted dedicated pool or a private VPC-connected deployment; we can scope both but pilot will use hosted-dedicated to move fast.

[07:10] Carlos: cost is material — if we can get predictable per-token spend by proving batching & KV cache benefits, that's helpful. also curious about quantization tradeoffs — we've seen small artifacts with int8 on long responses.

[07:45] Ethan: we'll capture that in the benchmark matrix. plan is to run two model variants: 1) FP16 baseline and 2) int8/4-bit quantized to measure cost savings vs quality delta. we'll include a sampling of your longest tail requests.

[09:00] Aisha: how do you handle kv cache across concurrent sessions? our traffic has many repeated prefixes (same ship ids).

[09:20] Ethan: we have prefix caching and automatic kv retention policies; the benchmark will include a prefix-hit scenario to quantify token savings and latency improvements. We'll ask you to label repeated sessions in the replay if possible.

[10:40] Maya: let's talk traffic modeling specifics we need from you: 7-day replay with timestamps, input token counts, output token counts, per-request latency goal flag, and a 1-week histogram of peak minute qps. can you provide that?

[11:02] Aisha: yes, we can. will anonymize identifiers. export should be a gzipped csv?

[11:08] Liam: gzipped CSV or parquet is fine. we'll add a token_hist.json with percentiles.

[12:30] Carlos: timeline — we want pilot in next 4 weeks, production by Q3. thought process: 1 week to prep data & configs, 1 week to run synthetic benchmarks, 2 weeks live shadow and quality checks. is that realistic?

[12:55] Ethan: that's aggressive but doable if we have the replay and network peering ready quickly. we'll aim for 3-week pilot: week 0 prep, week 1 synthetic stress + quantization sweep, week 2 live shadowing and acceptance.

[14:20] Aisha: acceptance criteria — e2e p50/p95/p99 numbers, and qualitative model output checks (fewer than X hallucinations per 10k requests). we also want cost per 1M tokens below your expected number — we'll put a target.

[15:05] Maya: agree. propose acceptance: p99 model-side <= 420ms on peak bursts, throughput sustain >= 1.2x peak qps for 5 min windows, and no more than 2 severe quality regressions per 10k queries. we document all metrics in the benchmark-template.

[16:30] Carlos: sounds good. any special security requirements? we need SOC2 aligned audit logs and KMS integration for keys.

[16:50] Liam: and data residency — some driver PII must not leave us-east1; can we pin regions?

[17:18] Ethan: Redwood supports region pinning and KMS integrations; we do provide audit logs and can enable tenant-level encryption. for pilot we'll use dedicated hosted capacity in us-east1 to satisfy residency. we'll send the SOC2 and security whitepaper.

[19:00] Aisha: what about concurrency model during the benchmark? we have spikes where concurrency across sessions jumps — how do you emulate that?

[19:25] Ethan: we'll create a synthetic driver that replays timestamps preserved to reproduce burst windows; concurrency will be controlled by client concurrency flags. we'll run a ramp and a burst 5x the baseline for 10 minutes to measure tail.

[20:45] Maya: metrics we will report: model-side p50/p95/p99 latency, token throughput (tokens/sec), tokens saved via cache (prefix hit rate), qps sustainable, CPU/GPU utilization, and cost estimate per million tokens. also qualitative sample outputs.

[24:10] Carlos: are you able to trace per-request tokenization differences? sometimes our preprocessor tokenizes differently.

[24:28] Ethan: yes — in the replay we'll take raw text and run redwood tokenizer to compute token counts; we'll report both original and normalized token counts.

[27:00] Aisha: for long outputs (300-400 tokens) we worry about stepwise decoding times — does your runtime support streaming so drivers see incremental responses?

[27:20] Ethan: yes, streaming is supported; we'll measure time to first token and time to final token. first token latency is usually much lower than full-generation latency; we'll include both as separate KPIs.

[30:40] Maya: ok let's define the benchmark matrix quickly: baseline (fp16, no cache), cache-enabled (fp16 + prefix cache), quantized (int8/4-bit + cache), and sample quality checks for each bucket. we will also include a dropout test where we cut GPU capacity to simulate noisy neighbors.

[33:15] Carlos: we also want to see cold-start behavior for rarely used routes; some route types might have stateful prompts that increase token length.

[33:45] Ethan: we'll add a cold-start test with isolated sessions and measure warmup and kv priming penalties.

[36:00] Liam: network egress — can you provide an estimate for egress per million requests? we need that for cost analysis.

[36:20] Maya: yes we'll include egress bytes per call and cost model. we'll include both hosted and private deployment egress scenarios.

[39:10] Aisha: what's the plan for model rollbacks during live shadowing if quality degrades?

[39:25] Ethan: we'll instrument automatic fallback policies and a canary rollback. during pilot we'll run traffic in shadow mode and then cutover to canary with gradual ramp, if regressions detected we roll back to baseline instantly. all configuration in the rollout plan doc.

[42:00] Maya: next up — deliverables and owners: maya to send benchmark-template and playbook link, ethan to prepare model configs and quantization matrix, aisha to produce the replay and token histograms, liam to confirm network peering.

[42:35] Carlos: ok, also can you run an initial quick smoke test on a 1-hour run so we can see rough numbers before full replay?

[42:50] Ethan: yes — we can do a 1-hour smoke during the prep week. we'll schedule for 2027-05-24 02:00 UTC (per your low-traffic window).

[45:10] Aisha: on quality checks — we'll provide a small labeled test set (200 examples) for automated regression detection. we want to see BLEU-ish scores or human-annotator flags.

[46:02] Maya: we support configurable eval hooks; attach your annotator sheet and we'll integrate with the quality dashboard.

[48:30] Carlos: any blockers we foresee? vendor lock-in concerns, quantization fidelity, and peering setup timing.

[48:50] Maya: we'll document migration path and fallback to public models; for quantization fidelity we'll show sample diffs and allow you to review. peering is the main ops task on your end.

[52:00] Liam: timeline for SOC2 doc? we need to review before signing off on private endpoints.

[52:20] Ethan: we'll send the SOC2 artifact and the security pack by EOD.

[54:00] Maya: recap of acceptance criteria: model-side p99 <= 420ms during peak bursts, sustain 1.2x peak QPS for 5-min bursts, cost target TBD but we'll estimate, and quality regressions below threshold. agreed?

[54:30] Carlos: agreed.
[55:00] Aisha: agreed.
[55:10] Liam: agreed.

[56:00] Maya: ok action owners and dates — i'll follow up with the spreadsheet and a calendar invite for the smoke test and the benchmark run.

[57:20] Carlos: thanks — we'll get the replay and histograms out by Friday.

[58:40] Ethan: quick note — competitors like anthropic/vertex are being evaluated in parallel, but you mentioned you prefer a partner that can do dedicated capacity + strong observability. hope that positions us well.

[60:00] Maya: thanks everyone. end of call.
